problems.title: The best-checkpoint option selects current rather than best state
problems.source_location: finetuning.py, lines 12–37 and 155–161; utils.py, get_finetuning_state_dict; current author commit 9b83bf208a124eb9d33f7a680d7924f1f1700953
claim: Both final-save branches serialize the current model. The best-validation state is also captured without an immutable copy.
analysis: Take consecutive parameter states \((1,2,3)\) with validation scores \((1,0,0)\), and enable best-state saving. The highest score is at state \(1\), but the shared final expression serializes state \(3\). Reference-based capture can also change while training storage is updated; the ignored best-state object already establishes failure independently of aliasing. Final-best and final-state-only settings are passing cases.
result: The public option does not ensure the saved checkpoint corresponds to its printed best score. The paper does not promise this exact selection rule, and historical use is unresolved.
repair: Capture an immutable selected state, metric and step when validation improves; serialize that snapshot when requested, with explicit no-validation and tie handling.
problems.existing_correction_status: A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a public optional checkpoint-selection defect, not evidence that reported paper checkpoints were selected through it.

problems.title: Validation does not restore the subsequent training mode
problems.source_location: finetuning.py, train_epoch, lines 12–37, and eval_dataset, lines 40–62; current author commit 9b83bf208a124eb9d33f7a680d7924f1f1700953
claim: The epoch sets training mode once; periodic validation sets evaluation mode and never restores it before later optimization batches.
analysis: With three training batches and validation every two, the control flow gives forward modes \((\mathrm{train},\mathrm{train},\mathrm{eval})\). Mode changes do not disable backpropagation. For scalar prediction \(dw\) with inverted dropout \(d=M/(1-p)\), squared loss has expected training gradient \(w/(1-p)-y\), whereas evaluation mode gives \(w-y\). At \(p=1/2\), \(w=1\), \(y=0\), these are \(2\) and \(1\). Zero dropout or validation only after the final batch removes this particular effect.
result: The current source changes the optimization distribution after validation. The direction or size of any LoRA/full-tuning performance effect is not established.
repair: Save the caller’s mode, evaluate without gradient tracking, and restore that mode on every return or exception. Intentionally mixed child-module modes require corresponding per-module restoration.
problems.existing_correction_status: A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a release training-protocol defect, with original generating-code correspondence and empirical consequences unverified.

problems.title: Asymmetric reference rounding can create a zero-update intruder
problems.source_location: Definition 3.1 and Algorithm 1, PDF p.4; find_intruder_dimensions.py, lines 12–17 and 34–40; utils.py, get_model_to_train
claim: The public entry point first loads the reference in float16 while the tuned-model helper defaults to float32. Casting both to float32 immediately before SVD cannot recover the lost reference entries.
analysis: Take identical original matrices \(W=(1-c)I_{16}+c\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\), with stored diagonal \(1\) and off-diagonal \(c\approx2\times10^{-8}\). The leading vector is \(q=\mathbf1/4\), with simple spectral gap \(16c\). Since \(0<c<2^{-25}\), half-precision round-to-nearest erases each off-diagonal entry, yielding identity. A valid identity SVD uses coordinate vectors, giving \(\max_i|q^\top e_i|=1/4<1/2\): one top-vector intruder despite zero actual tuning update. Equal original inputs instead give cosine \(1\) and count zero. The rounded repeated spectrum makes the outcome basis-dependent; no universal backend result or frequency in real model layers is claimed.
result: The current measurement path admits a precision-history false positive. It does not establish that the observed original intruders or behavioral interventions are all numerical artifacts.
repair: Load both original matrices from the same model revision at equal original analysis precision, retain dtype/hash/gap diagnostics, and include a zero-update control. Equalizing dtype after one-sided rounding is insufficient; repeated-spectrum subspace interpretation remains a separate question.
problems.existing_correction_status: A proposed correction is described; author adoption is not established.
problems.impact_rationale: This is a current public diagnostic-path counterexample, with no established occurrence or quantitative impact in the paper’s actual checkpoint matrices.
